title: Contract slice overprovision scenarios — Aug 2028
content:
Purpose:
Quick simulation notes to test a lightweight overprovision strategy for per-contract dedicated GPU slices. Trying to find minimal safe overprovision factors per region that avoid hard throttles during short spikes (2–6 hours) while keeping overall fleet overhead < 12%.

Summary (top-line):
- Baseline committed capacity across active contracts: 2,720 GPUs (sum of all committed slabs).
- Observed historical 95th-percentile burst factor by region: us-west 1.35, us-east 1.28, eu-west 1.30, ap-east 1.55 (sparse but high).
- Target fleet overprovision budget: 11% total spare beyond commitments to cover 95th percentile short bursts plus cross-region relocation buffer.

Assumptions / inputs: (pull from billing/usage slices and the incident logs linked above)
- Lookback window: last 180 days of per-contract peak usage (1h rolling)
- We assume contracts have an elasticity bucket (burst allowed) only if they paid for burst add-on; otherwise strict commit. List of contracts with burst: CON-17, CON-21, CON-34, CON-42.
- Time-to-shift (cross-region relocation) = 45 minutes median (pack + migrate KV cache warmup + routing update).
- If region saturates, automatic fallback to secondary region allowed for 62% of contracts. The rest require manual approval.

Scenario table (simulated):
Contract | Committed GPUs | Region | 95p peak multiple | Overprov factor (p) | Effective buffer GPUs | Notes
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CON-17   |  320           | us-west | 1.40              | 1.10               | 32                    | high burst customer, paid burst add-on
CON-21   |  120           | eu-west | 1.20              | 1.05               | 6                     | can fallback to us-east
CON-34   |  640           | us-east | 1.30              | 1.08               | 51                    | steady daytime usage, spikes nights
CON-42   |  240           | ap-east | 1.60              | 1.20               | 48                    | extreme spikes, exploratory AI lab
CON-88   |  96            | us-west | 1.10              | 1.00               | 0                     | low priority, no burst
CON-99   |  256           | eu-west | 1.25              | 1.06               | 16                    | can tolerate 500ms extra latency

Total committed (subset) = 1,672 GPUs, implied overprov buffer used = 153 GPUs (9.15% for subset).

Notes on overprov factor selection (p):
- p chosen = max(1.0, min(1.25, ceil(95p-peak * 100)/100)) but also capped by contract SLA tier and fleet budget.
- For contracts with explicit burst entitlement, we allowed p up to 1.20. For others, p<=1.08 by policy.

Micro-sim results (72hr synthetic run, input trace sampling + poisson noise):
- Run A (no overprov): 14 of 72 hours had at least one contract hard-throttled -> user-visible 503s simulated.
- Run B (11% global spare, region-weighted allocation): 3 of 72 hours had soft-degrades (queueing) but zero hard-throttles.
- Run C (conservative per-contract p=1.15 for all burst-eligible): 0 hard-throttles but fleet spare = 15.6% (exceeds budget).

Region breakdown (after allocation):
- us-west: committed 1,024 -> allocated spare 95 (9.3%) -> peak headroom covers 95p of historical spikes except extreme weekends.
- us-east: committed 832 -> allocated spare 68 (8.2%) -> fallback enabled for 70% of contracts.
- eu-west: committed 512 -> allocated spare 42 (8.2%) -> cross-region east fallback planned.
- ap-east: committed 352 -> allocated spare 80 (22.7%) -> hotspot, explains high empty headroom cost.

Actionable recommendations (short):
1) Apply region-weighted overprovision policy: target global spare 11% but move allocation to ap-east to 18% to cover measured variance. Reserved spare tokens tracked as "reserved-burst" feature in billing.
2) For top-10 contracts by committed GPUs, create individual 95p spike contracts (15-min granularity) and offer a paid burst addon that caps p at 1.20. Default to manual opt-in.
3) Implement a micro-eviction policy for very short (<30m) KV-warm caches to free up ephemeral GPUs during sudden spikes, measurable via tracing hook INF-TRACE-evict-2.
4) Add automation to run the 72h synthetic micro-sim weekly after the nightly ingestion job (script at linked PR).

Open questions / things to validate:
- How many contracts will opt into paid burst vs require auto-fallback? Ask sales & CSM to survey top 25 (Sophie/Priya).
- Confirm ap-east procurement runway — 22% spare there increases fleet cost by ~3.2% q/q (finance check).
- Need tighter definition of "soft-degrade" for SLA measurement (is increased latency acceptable or do we mark as incident?).

Quick TODOs (owner):
- Marco: wire the per-contract trace window into capacity-sim (PR #87) and rerun with full customer set (ETA 2028-07-20).
- Sophie: brief sales on paid burst offer and price bands (by 2028-07-18).
- Jamal: draft automation for weekly micro-sim and add telemetry hooks (INF-TRACE-evict-2 + INF-SIM-telemetry) (ETA 2028-07-25).

Notes to self / ephemeral thoughts:
- Might be worth exploring a short-term marketplace for swapping spare GPUs across tenants within same legal boundary for extreme weekends (manual ops; emergency only).
- If we push ap-east headroom down, watch for longer cache-warm times — more downstream cold start errors.
- Slack thread: #infra-dedicated-capacity -> see pinned message (link pasted into Confluence page CONFLUENCE-2345).

Raw sample calculation (CON-34):
- committed = 640
- observed 95p peak multiplier = 1.30 -> peak would be 832 GPUs if unconstrained
- chosen p = 1.08 -> allowed = 691 (rounded) -> buffer = 51 GPUs -> if buffer exhausted -> fallback to us-west (allowed) or queue

Appendix: quick list of linked artifacts and logs used:
- billing/capacity/export/2028-07-01..2028-07-04 (snapshot)
- JIRA-INFRA-1228 (ap-east procurement notes)
- github.com/redwood-inference/capacity-sim (PR/87)

End of doc — this is a working note, not final. Expect followups after full-run sim and finance check.
